“It is a most peculiar sort of inheritance, I must admit,” said I, gesturing towards the object which lay upon our mantelpiece. “A cracked teacup seems a poor legacy to leave one’s only friend.”

“And yet, my dear Croft, it is the most illuminating legacy our late neighbour could have possibly bequeathed,” replied Alistair Finch, without looking up from his armchair. “Mrs. Gable was quite distressed when she brought it to me this morning, believing Mr. Abernathy’s nephew had carelessly abandoned his uncle’s last possession. The young man, it seems, was in a great hurry to depart after the reading of the will.”

“And what did you tell her?”

“That the nephew had not abandoned it at all; on the contrary, he had made a frantic, last minute attempt to destroy it. She found the pieces, you see, not on the table, but stuffed deep into the coal scuttle, moments before she was to replenish the fire. It was she who painstakingly glued it back together, thinking it an act of sentiment.”

“To destroy it? But why? It is a worthless thing.”

“That, my friend, is where you are mistaken. It is the key to understanding why a man of comfortable, if not extravagant, means should leave his entire estate to a charitable fund for indigent artists, and to his own flesh and blood, only this.”

He rose and took the cup in his long, slender fingers, holding it to the light. It was a common piece of porcelain, white with a simple pattern of blue willows, but webbed with a dozen cracks where it had been crudely mended.

“What can you, a man of medicine, discern from it yourself?” he asked.

I took the cup and turned it over. “Very little. The handle has been stained brown, as if by constant use. There are coffee dregs, not tea, in the bottom. The mending is amateurish. It is, as I said, a perfectly ordinary, broken cup.”

“You see the facts, but not the story,” he said, reclaiming his prize. “You are too modest in your conclusions. It is perfectly plain, for instance, that Mr. Abernathy was a man of intensely rigid habits, that he suffered from a nervous affliction which worsened over the last year, and that he had a profound secret which he guarded even from his own family.”

“Alistair, you are inventing a narrative! From a teacup?”

“From the evidence,” he corrected me gently. “Here is my lens. Observe the base of the handle. You called the stain brown; I call it nicotine. It is deeply ingrained, showing that he held his cup in the same hand as his cigarette, a habit formed over many, many years. A man of rigid routine.”

“That is plausible enough,” I conceded.

“Now, look at the rim. Here, and here.” He pointed to two tiny chips on the lip of the cup, directly opposite the handle. “These are not cracks from the object’s general destruction. They are small, repeated impacts. A man’s teeth chattering against the porcelain, not once, but often. This began recently, for the chips are sharp and not worn down by subsequent washing. His nerves, therefore, have failed him only in the last year or so.”

“And the great secret?” I asked, a smile playing on my lips.

“Ah, that is the most fascinating part. Why would his nephew, who by all accounts is a respectable young clerk, wish to destroy it? Not for its value. He wishes to destroy the association. The cup is not Abernathy’s primary cup; it is his only cup. Notice the utter absence of any other porcelain in his rooms, a fact Mrs. Gable confirmed. He drank everything from this single vessel. Why? Because it was not originally his.”

He turned the cup so that its base was visible. There, in the very centre, was a small maker’s mark, almost entirely worn away. But beside it, scratched crudely into the glaze with a pin or a knife point, were two initials: ‘L. M.’

“‘L. M.’!” I exclaimed. “Not Abernathy.”

“Precisely. He adopted an object that belonged to someone else, and it became a totem, a relic. The nephew knew this. He knew what, or who, ‘L. M.’ was, and he wanted the final piece of evidence connecting his uncle to this person utterly obliterated. The question is, what became of the original owner?”

“Well,” said I, laughing, “since there is no crime, and the man is unfortunately deceased, I suppose we shall never know. Your deductions are ingenious, Alistair, but they lead us nowhere.”

“Perhaps not nowhere,” Finch murmured, his eyes glinting. He had produced a small jeweller’s tool from his pocket and was now delicately probing the largest crack near the base of the cup, where a sliver of the porcelain had flaked away. “The glue Mrs. Gable used is cheap and brittle. It has not quite filled every crevice. There is something caught deep within the fracture. Something that is not pottery.”

With the deftness of a surgeon, he worked the point of his tool into the crack. A tiny, dark object came loose and fell onto the white linen of the tablecloth. It was not a splinter or a speck of dust. It was a triangular shard of dried, blackened material.

Finch picked it up with his tweezers and placed it under the lens of his powerful desk lamp. He was silent for a full minute, his face a mask of concentration.

“Good heavens,” he whispered at last, straightening up.

“What is it, Finch? What have you found?”

He looked at me, and all trace of intellectual amusement had vanished from his face, replaced by a grim severity I had not seen in months.

“Get your coat, Croft,” he said, his voice low and urgent. “This is a matter for the police, and a serious one at that. Unless I am very much mistaken, this is a fragment of a human fingernail.”

And it proves, once again, that in the quest for truth, one should never, ever neglect the humble goose.”

The choice is yours.”

“It is incredible, Holmes! Staggering!” I cried. “And Mr. Baker?”

“Ah, Mr. Baker,” said Holmes, picking up the three half-crowns from the mantelpiece. “I believe this will cover the cost of his advertisement, with a little left over. As for his future, Mycroft’s gratitude is not without its practical uses. I believe the British Museum will find it has a sudden and urgent need for a translator of obscure classical texts. He reached for his violin, but this time, the melody that filled the air was light and triumphant, a joyful, dancing tune that spoke of a puzzle solved, a danger averted, and the strange, intricate, and wonderful tapestry of life as seen from our windows at 221B Baker Street.

This, unless I am much mistaken, is the blue carbuncle, the famous gem of the Countess of Morcar, which was lost a week ago.” I had sprung to my feet at Holmes’s exclamation, and stood staring in utter bewilderment at the brilliant jewel which lay upon the commissionaire’s calloused palm. Peterson, for his part, looked from one to the other of us, his mouth agape, the full import of his discovery only just dawning upon his simple and honest soul. “The Countess of Morcar’s carbuncle!” I stammered. “Why, Holmes, the papers have been full of nothing else! It was valued at more than twenty thousand pounds.” “Precisely,” said Holmes, his eyes gleaming with that peculiar light which I had come to associate with the scent of a new and intricate problem. “The reward offered is a thousand pounds. A very tidy sum for a Christmas windfall, eh, Peterson?” The commissionaire swallowed hard, his gaze fixed upon the stone as if mesmerized. “A thousand pounds, Mr. Holmes!” he breathed. “Good Lord! My wife and I… we could…” “Quite so,” Holmes interrupted, his tone becoming brisk and businesslike. “But before we consider the division of the spoils, we must first consider the problem of the thief. This stone, Peterson, is not merely a treasure; it is a clue. It is the missing link in a chain of events which began with a simple assault in the street and has now landed us in the midst of a grand larceny. You have done well, exceptionally well, to bring it to me. Your part in this affair is over, save for the pleasant duty of collecting your reward. I shall see to it that your claim is recognized. Now, I must ask you to leave me, for I have a great deal to think about.” With a few more words of bewildered thanks and promises to follow Mr. Holmes’s instructions to the letter, the commissionaire departed, leaving the blue carbuncle upon the edge of the table. Holmes picked it up and held it to the light, his long, thin fingers turning it over and over. “A fascinating object, Watson,” he remarked. “Beautiful, certainly, but also a magnet for trouble. It has been the source of at least two crimes in the last week: a robbery at the Hotel Cosmopolitan, and the wrongful imprisonment of a man named John Horner.” “The plumber who was accused of the theft?” I asked. “The very same. He was arrested on the testimony of the head attendant, a man named James Ryder, who claimed to have seen Horner in the Countess’s suite shortly before the jewel was missed. Horner has a previous conviction, which naturally made him the prime suspect for the police. But I have never been convinced of his guilt. The evidence was too neat, too convenient.” “And now this,” I said, gesturing towards the stone. “This proves his innocence.” “It proves that the jewel was not in his possession, at any rate,” Holmes corrected. “It was, until this morning, in the crop of a goose belonging to a Mr. Henry Baker. And the question we must now answer is, how did it get there?” He had been pacing the room as he spoke, his hands clased behind his back, his head sunk upon his chest. Now he stopped and looked at me, his grey eyes alight with intellectual excitement. “There is only one logical explanation, Watson. The thief, whoever he is, must have sought a way to conceal the stone. What better hiding place than the gullet of a bird destined for the Christmas table? It is a stroke of criminal genius, audacious and yet strangely practical. But fate, as is so often the case, has intervened. The thief has lost his goose, and we have found his jewel.” “But who is the thief?” I persisted. “That, my dear Watson, is what we are about to find out. The trail begins with Mr. Henry Baker and his unfortunate Christmas dinner. We must find him, and we must do so without delay. For while we sit here, an innocent man languishes in prison, and a desperate criminal is searching frantically for a bird which no longer exists.” “But you said yourself that finding one Henry Baker among thousands is an impossible task.” “It was an impossible task when all we had was a hat,” said Holmes with a smile. “Now, however, we have a new line of inquiry. The goose. Where did it come from? All geese of a certain quality sold in London come from a limited number of suppliers. I shall place an advertisement in all the evening papers. It is a long shot, but it is our only shot.” He scribbled a few lines on a piece of paper and handed it to me. “Read that.” I took the paper and read: “Found at the corner of Goodge Street, a Christmas goose and a black felt hat. Mr. Henry Baker can have the same by applying at 6:30 this evening at 221B, Baker Street.” “But the goose is gone,” I objected. “He will expect to receive the bird as well as the hat.” “Precisely,” said Holmes. “And when he finds that we cannot produce it, he will be forced to explain its provenance. We will offer him a new goose, a finer goose, as compensation. But in return, he must tell us where he purchased the original. From that point, the trail will be clear.” “It is ingenious,” I admitted. “But what if he does not see the advertisement?” “He will see it,” said Holmes with conviction. “A man who has lost a twenty pound dinner is not likely to give up the search easily. He will be scanning the papers for any news of his lost property. Now, Watson, I must ask you to go out and place these advertisements for me. And while you are at it, perhaps you could procure a fine, plump goose from the poulterer’s. We must have a replacement ready when our visitor arrives.” I spent the afternoon carrying out Holmes’s instructions, my mind buzzing with the strange twists and turns of the case. The thought that a magnificent jewel, a stone of royalty, had made its way across London inside a common Christmas goose was almost too fantastic to be believed. And yet, as I had learned so many times before, the most fantastic events were often the most logical when viewed through the lens of my friend’s extraordinary intellect. When I returned to Baker Street, I found Holmes deep in conversation with a man who could only be our long awaited visitor. He was a large man, with a broad, honest face, a tweed suit that had seen better days, and the very same battered hat that had been the subject of Holmes’s remarkable deductions held nervously in his hands. “Ah, Watson, you are just in time,” said Holmes, looking up as I entered. “This is Mr. Henry Baker, the gentleman whose property we have had the good fortune to recover.” Mr. Baker bowed awkwardly, a look of profound relief on his face. “I am most grateful to you, Mr. Holmes,” he said in a deep, rumbling voice. “I had quite given up hope of ever seeing my hat again. And the goose, too… it was a fine bird. I had been looking forward to it.” “I am afraid there has been a slight complication regarding the goose, Mr. Baker,” said Holmes, his tone carefully modulated. “You see, we believed it was best to eat it before it went bad. However, we have purchased a replacement for you, which I trust you will find to be of equal or even superior quality.” He gestured to the plump bird which I had placed upon the sideboard. Mr. Baker’s face fell. “Oh,” he said. “Well, that is very kind of you, sir. But it is not quite the same, is it? You see, that particular goose was part of a goose club I belong to. I was supposed to pay a few pence a week, and then I would get my bird at Christmas. It was a special arrangement.” “I see,” said Holmes, leaning forward slightly. “A goose club. And where is this club to be found?” “It is run by the landlord of the Alpha Inn, near the British Museum,” said Mr. Baker. “A very respectable establishment. He gets his geese from a dealer in Covent Garden.” “And did you know this dealer’s name?” Holmes asked, his voice casual. “I believe so,” said Mr. Baker, scratching his head. “A Mr. Breckinridge, if I recall correctly. He has a stall in the main market.” “Thank you, Mr. Baker,” said Holmes, standing up. “You have been most helpful. I trust this new goose will provide you with a satisfactory dinner. And I am delighted to have been able to restore your hat to you.” After Mr. Baker had departed, clutching his new goose and his old hat, Holmes turned to me, his face a mask of grim satisfaction. “The trail is hot, Watson,” he said, grabbing his coat and hat. “To the Alpha Inn, and then to Covent Garden. We must find this Breckinridge before our quarry doubles back on his tracks.” Our inquiries at the Alpha Inn confirmed Mr. Baker’s story. The landlord, a portly and garrulous man, was happy to tell us all about his goose club and his supplier, Mr. Breckinridge. He even showed us his ledger, which listed the names of all the members, including Mr. Henry Baker. From there, we took a cab to Covent Garden, the bustling heart of London’s produce trade. The market was a cacophony of sights and sounds, a vibrant tapestry of human activity. But Holmes had no time for sightseeing. He strode through the crowds with a purposeful air, his keen eyes scanning the stalls until he found the one we were looking for: a large poulterer’s stand with the name “Breckinridge” painted in large letters above it. The proprietor was a man with a face like a bulldog, red cheeked and belligerent. He was in the midst of a heated argument with a small, weaselly man whose face was pale with anxiety. As we approached, we overheard their conversation. “I have told you a dozen times, I have sold them all!” the poulterer was shouting. “They are all gone! To Mr. Windigate of the Alpha Inn.” “But you must have one left!” the little man pleaded, his voice thin and reedy. “I will pay you double, triple! I must have one of those geese!” “Get out of my sight!” roared Breckinridge. “I am a busy man. I have no time for lunatics.” The little man scurried away, his shoulders slumped in defeat. Holmes watched him go, a thoughtful expression on his face. Then he turned to the poulterer, who was now glowering at a crate of chickens. “Excuse me,” said Holmes, his voice calm and authoritative. “I believe you can help me.” Breckinridge turned his surly gaze upon us. “And who might you be?” he demanded. “My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people do not know.” “Well, you can know this,” sneered Breckinridge. “I am tired of being pestered about geese. First that little weasel, and now you. What is it you want?” “I want to know where you got the geese you sold to Mr. Windigate.” “If you want to know that, you can buy it,” the man retorted, a crafty look in his eye. “It is my business, and I expect to be paid for my information.” “How much?” asked Holmes. “A guinea.” Holmes drew a sovereign from his pocket and tossed it onto the counter. “There you are. Now, no more prevarication. From whom did you buy those geese?” Breckinridge’s truculent manner softened at the sight of the gold coin. He scooped it up and pointed to a ledger at his side. “You can see for yourself,” he said. “I keep a record of all my dealings. Here we are. Oakshott, of Brixton Road. I bought a flock of two dozen from him this week.” “And the address?” “43, Prothero Street. But I doubt you will find him there now. He has likely gone back to the country.” “One last question,” said Holmes. “The little man who was here just now. You told him that you had sold the geese to Mr. Windigate. Did you tell him anything else?” “I told him he was a fool and that I was sick of the sight of him,” Breckinridge grumbled. “He has been here every day, asking the same questions.” “I see,” said Holmes. He turned to me, his face grim. “Come, Watson. Our business here is done, but I fear the most dangerous part is yet to come. That little man was not asking for his health. He is the one we seek. He is the one who put the stone into the goose.” “But who is he?” I asked as we hurried through the crowded market. “His name, I suspect, is James Ryder,” said Holmes. “He is the head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. The very man who gave evidence against John Horner, pointing the finger of suspicion at the plumber. It is a classic case of misdirection, Watson. Ryder stole the jewel himself. Panicking, he sought a way to smuggle it out of the hotel. He went to his sister’s house, a Mrs. Oakshott, who raises geese. He thrust the stone down the throat of one of her finest birds, intending to retrieve it later. But in a twist of fate that even I could not have invented, his sister had promised that very bird to Mr. Breckinridge for his Christmas sales. Ryder, arriving too late, found the flock gone. And he has been on a desperate, frantic chase ever since, a chase that has now led us right to his doorstep. To Prothero Street, Watson! And let us hope we are not too late!”

Our mad dash through the cobbled alleys of Covent Garden ended with a sharp cry from Holmes, who hailed a passing hansom with an imperious wave of his cane. The cabbie, a grizzled fellow with a face weathered by a thousand London winters, pulled his horse up sharply, a look of mild surprise on his face. “Prothero Street, Brixton!” Holmes called out, pushing me into the cab before vaulting in beside me. “And there is an extra half sovereign for you if you can get us there in twenty minutes!” The driver needed no further encouragement. With a crack of his whip and a shout to his horse, we lurched forward, plunging into the thick stream of afternoon traffic. The city was a blur of motion outside the rattling windows of the cab; carts and carriages vied for space, pedestrians darted across the muddy streets, and the gas lamps, just beginning to be lit against the gathering dusk, cast a pale, uncertain glow upon the bustling scene. “Consider the man’s mind, Watson,” Holmes said, breaking the silence. He had settled back against the leather squabs, his long legs stretched out before him, but his mind, I knew, was racing as fast as the wheels of our cab. “For a week, James Ryder has been living in a private hell. He has committed a great crime, and he has framed an innocent man for it. He believes he has secured his escape, his fortune, in the body of a goose. And then, at the last moment, his prize is snatched away from him. He goes to his sister, Mrs. Oakshott, to claim his bird, only to find it has been sold. Imagine the cold dread that must have seized him then.” “He must have been frantic,” I agreed. “Frantic is not the word for it,” said Holmes. “He is a man possessed. He would have rushed to the dealer, Breckinridge, only to be told that the geese have been sold again, this time to the Alpha Inn. He goes to the Alpha Inn, and what does he find? A goose club. Two dozen geese, distributed among two dozen members. His single, priceless goose is now lost in a flock of two dozen, and he has no way of knowing which is which.” I saw it all then, the whole desperate, pathetic chase. “So he has been trying to track down every member of the club,” I said. “Exactly. Pestering the landlord, haunting the neighbourhood, making a general nuisance of himself. And all for nothing. The one man who could have helped him, Mr. Henry Baker, had the misfortune to be set upon by ruffians and lose his prize before he even got it home. The trail went cold, and Ryder was left with nothing but his terror.” The cab clattered over a bridge, the dark, sluggish water of the Thames flowing beneath us. The grand buildings of the city centre gave way to the more modest, uniform streets of the southern suburbs. The air grew colder, and a light mist began to fall, blurring the edges of the gaslight and lending a ghostly, spectral quality to the rows of brick houses. “We are close now,” said Holmes, leaning forward to peer out of the window. “Prothero Street is just ahead. And with any luck, we shall find our man at home, nursing his despair.” The cab slowed to a halt at the end of a quiet, respectable looking street. Holmes paid the driver, adding the promised bonus, and we stepped out into the damp evening air. Number 43 was a neat, two storey house, indistinguishable from its neighbours save for a faint light glowing in an upstairs window. A sense of grim anticipation settled over me as we walked up the short path to the front door. This was the end of the chase, the final act in a drama that had begun with a lost hat and had now led us to the threshold of a thief. Holmes raised his hand and knocked, a sharp, decisive rap that echoed in the quiet street. We waited. For a long moment, there was no response. Then we heard a shuffling sound from within, the drawing of a bolt, and the door creaked open a few inches. A man’s face appeared in the gap, a face as white as a sheet, with wild, staring eyes and a tremor in the thin line of his lips. It was the same weaselly man we had seen at Breckinridge’s stall. “What do you want?” he asked, his voice a hoarse whisper. Holmes looked at him, his gaze steady and penetrating. “I think, Mr. Ryder,” he said softly, “that you are the man who is looking for a goose.” The effect of these words was extraordinary. James Ryder gave a strangled cry, as if he had been struck, and staggered back, his hand clutching at his throat. He would have fallen if Holmes had not pushed the door open and caught him by the arm. “Steady, man,” he said, his voice not unkind. “There is no need for hysterics. We are not the police. We have come to talk.” We helped the trembling man into a small, sparsely furnished parlour. He collapsed into a threadbare armchair by the cold hearth, his face buried in his hands, his body wracked with shuddering sobs. It was a pathetic sight, and I felt a pang of pity for this wretched creature, brought so low by his own greed and fear. Holmes stood over him, a tall, implacable figure in the dim light of the single oil lamp. “It is all over, Ryder,” he said, his voice firm but not harsh. “The game is up. We have the stone.” Ryder’s head snapped up at that, his eyes wide with a mixture of terror and disbelief. “The stone?” he croaked. “You found it?” “We found it,” said Holmes. “In the crop of a goose that was sold to a Mr. Henry Baker. A goose with a black bar across its tail, I believe.” At this final, crushing proof of our knowledge, Ryder’s last vestige of resistance crumbled. He let out a long, wailing moan and fell to his knees before my friend, clutching at the hem of his coat. “Mercy, Mr. Holmes!” he cried. “Have mercy! I never meant for it to go this far. I swear I did not!” “Get up, man,” said Holmes, pulling his coat away with a gesture of distaste. “Groveling will not help you. Your only hope is to make a full confession. Tell us everything, from the beginning.” And so, in a torrent of broken, self-pitying words, the whole sordid story came out. Ryder, a man of weak character and expensive tastes, had been tempted by the sight of the Countess of Morcar’s famous jewel. He had learned from the Countess’s maid, Catherine Cusack, that a plumber named John Horner, a man with a criminal record, was due to carry out some repairs in the suite. Seeing his chance, he had stolen the jewel, raised the alarm, and thrown suspicion upon the unfortunate Horner, knowing that the man’s past would make him an easy scapegoat. “But the police were searching everyone,” Ryder sobbed. “I knew they would search me. I had to get the stone out of the hotel. I thought of my sister, Maggie… Mrs. Oakshott. She lives here in Brixton. She raises geese for the market. I ran here, straight from the hotel, with the stone in my pocket.” “And you fed it to a goose,” said Holmes. “Yes, sir. There was a great flock of them in her yard. I caught the finest one I could see, a big, handsome bird with a black bar on its tail. I forced its beak open and pushed the stone down its throat. I thought it was safe. I told my sister I wanted that goose for my Christmas dinner, and she promised to save it for me.” “But she did not,” I interjected. “No, sir,” Ryder wailed. “She had another goose, just like it. Same size, same markings. She had promised one to Mr. Breckinridge in the market, and she got them mixed up. When I came to collect my bird, she gave me the wrong one. I did not realize it until I got it home and cut it open. It was empty. The stone was gone.” He wrung his hands in an agony of remembrance. “I ran back to my sister’s, but it was too late. She had sold the other goose. The one with the stone in it. I have been searching for it ever since, going from dealer to landlord, from house to house, but it was gone, lost forever. And all for nothing. I have betrayed my friends, sent an innocent man to gaol, and lost my own soul, and I have not even got the money.” He trailed off into a fit of hopeless weeping. For a long time, the only sound in the room was the ticking of a clock on the mantelpiece and the desperate, gulping sobs of the ruined man on the floor. Holmes stood motionless, his face in shadow, his expression unreadable. I wondered what he would do. The law was clear. This man was a thief, and he had callously condemned another to prison in his place. It was our duty to hand him over to the police. But as I looked at the broken figure before us, I confess that my heart was moved to pity. Finally, Holmes stirred. He walked to the door and threw it open, letting in a gust of cold, damp air. “Get out,” he said. Ryder looked up, his tear stained face a mask of confusion. “What did you say, sir?” “I said, get out,” Holmes repeated. “The door is open. The boat for the continent leaves from Tilbury at dawn. Be on it. Do not show your face in this country again. If you do, I shall see that you are arrested.” Ryder stared at him, his mouth open, unable to comprehend this sudden, unexpected reprieve. “You mean… you are letting me go?” “I am not a paid agent of the police,” said Holmes. “And this is Christmas. I suppose that I am commuting a felony, but I am just possibly saving a soul. You have been punished enough by your own fear. Now go, before I change my mind.” Without another word, James Ryder scrambled to his feet, grabbed his cap, and fled into the night, a furtive, hunted creature vanishing into the London mist. I looked at Holmes in astonishment. “You let him go, Holmes!” “The man is a coward, Watson,” he said, closing the door. “He will not return. He will spend the rest of his life looking over his shoulder, and that is a punishment far greater than any a court of law could impose.” “But what about Horner?” I asked. “The plumber who is in gaol.” “Ah, yes. Horner.” Holmes smiled, a rare, almost gentle expression softening the sharp lines of his face. “We must see that he is released. I shall have Peterson, the commissionaire, take the stone to the police. He can claim to have found it in the street, or some such tale. The police will have their jewel back, the Countess her bauble, and with the stone recovered, the case against Horner will collapse. Justice will be served, in its own roundabout way.” We took a cab back to Baker Street, the fire of our chase now banked and cooling. The streets were quieter now, the shops shuttered, the city settling down for the night. When we arrived back in our familiar rooms, Holmes lit his pipe and sank into his armchair, the blue carbuncle twinkling on the mantelpiece beside him. “A strange business, Watson,” he said, puffing a cloud of fragrant smoke into the air. “It began with a goose, and it ends with an act of mercy. A fitting tale for Christmastide, would you not agree?” “You have a singular sense of justice, Holmes,” I said, taking my own seat by the fire. “I simply try to see the world as it is, not as the lawbooks say it should be,” he replied. “For every effect, there is a cause.
